ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Harriet Tubman Synthetic CCD

text.paragraph: Primary care visit for lifelong headaches and sudden sleep spells. Concerns: Falls asleep without warning several times a day, which worries her family; Headaches most days have gotten worse over the past year despite daily ibuprofen; Wants to know whether the spells are seizures and does not want medicine that makes her duller. [S]

tr.td: Ibuprofen 200 mg oral tablet, two tablets by mouth most days (self-directed, over the counter)
Two tablets by mouth most days
Acetaminophen 500 mg oral tablet, two tablets by mouth as needed for headache, no more than 2 days a week
Two tablets by mouth as needed, at most 2 days a week
Candesartan 8 mg oral tablet, one tablet by mouth daily
Candesartan 16 mg oral tablet, one tablet by mouth daily
Modafinil 100 mg oral tablet, one tablet by mouth each morning
One tablet by mouth each morning

value.displayName: Drug-induced headache, not elsewhere classified, not intractable
Narcolepsy in conditions classified elsewhere without cataplexy

tr.td: Routine EEG: normal background with intermittent left frontal slowing; no epileptiform discharges
MRI of the brain: old depressed left frontal skull defect with small underlying encephalomalacia; normal hippocampi; no tumor or other lesion
Ambulatory EEG with video, 72 hours: four typical spells captured, each at sleep onset with no ictal pattern
Overnight polysomnography: apnea-hypopnea index 4 per hour; no periodic limb movements; REM sleep within 15 minutes of sleep onset
Multiple sleep latency test: mean sleep latency 4.5 minutes with two sleep-onset REM periods in five naps
Recombinant zoster vaccine, two-dose series completed

code.displayName: Pneumococcal conjugate PCV20, polysaccharide CRM197 conjugate, adjuvant, PF
RSV, recombinant, protein subunit RSVpreF, adjuvant reconstituted, 0.5 mL, PF

text.paragraph: Historical biography with true dates. These events are not part of the synthetic care timeline.

tr.td: Head injury in her early teens from an iron weight thrown by an overseer; nearly killed, with little or no medical care
Headaches and sudden spells of sleep with vivid dreams and visions since the injury, continuing into old age
Temporal lobe epilepsy proposed retrospectively as the cause of the spells; not established
Post-traumatic narcolepsy proposed retrospectively in 2023 as an alternative explanation; not established

tr.td: Primary care visit for lifelong headaches and sudden sleep spells
Neurology consultation with EEG and brain MRI
Review of ambulatory EEG and sleep studies; four-week headache check
Same-day sick visit for vomiting and diarrhea
Neurology referral for lifelong spells after a head injury, to decide whether they are seizures or sleep attacks
Obtain a routine EEG and brain MRI, then capture typical spells on ambulatory EEG with video; start antiseizure medicine only if the spells prove epileptic
Overnight polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test to evaluate excessive daytime sleepiness
Start modafinil 100 mg each morning with two scheduled 15-minute naps a day; check blood pressure and heart rate at follow-up
Stop daily ibuprofen, limit acute treatment to 2 days a week, and keep a headache diary
Start non-sedating headache prevention with candesartan, titrated after a potassium and creatinine check
Screen mood, anxiety, trauma symptoms, and cognition at baseline with a trauma-informed approach, and repeat the PHQ-9 at follow-up
Stop daily over-the-counter analgesics and limit acute headache medicine to no more than 2 days a week
No ibuprofen since the first visit; acetaminophen about once a week
Cut headache days by at least half by the three-month review
Headache days fell from 54 to 21 in three months
Reduce daytime sleep attacks and lower the PROMIS sleep-related impairment T-score below 60
T-score fell from 68 to 55; one or two planned naps a day and rare unplanned episodes
Establish whether the spells are epileptic before considering antiseizure medicine
Typical spells captured on ambulatory EEG were sleep onset; no antiseizure medicine needed
